screens.title: Case Studies: Modern Multiprocessors
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we study three families that shape modern servers: AMD EPYC, Intel Xeon, and ARM Neoverse. You will learn the defining architectural choices for each family — chiplets and Infinity Fabric for EPYC, tile and EMIB design plus AMX for Intel, and coherent mesh plus CXL expansion for ARM — and why those choices make a processor suitable for cloud, HPC, or AI workloads. We'll connect concrete hardware facts, like core counts, memory channels, and cache organizations, to practical outcomes: throughput on parallel benchmarks, latency for single-thread work, and efficiency for AI inference. As you explore, notice recurring trade-offs: raw core count versus single-thread performance, memory bandwidth versus input and output density, and the presence or absence of specialized accelerators. A concrete example: EPYC's 12 DDR5 channels support many cores in throughput-bound workloads, while Intel's AMX provides instruction-level acceleration for low-precision inference tasks. Common misconceptions to avoid are thinking more cores always give better performance and assuming AI acceleration replaces the need for memory bandwidth. By the end, you should be able to explain why a cloud provider might pick EPYC for throughput, Intel for mixed latency-plus-AI workloads, or ARM for power-sensitive large-scale deployments. Which design trade-off will matter most for your workload?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Applied Milestones
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives screen turns the learning targets into practical steps you can perform. First, after you can describe architectures, practice by annotating a processor's datasheet: identify CCDs, tiles, or the CMN-700 and list memory channels. That skill matters because it lets you spot bandwidth bottlenecks early. Second, for coherence and memory, practice comparing directory-based coherence and snooping: determine which domain uses a directory (between chiplets/tiles) and where snooping provides fast intra-die sharing. This clarifies why some workloads see lower cache miss penalties on certain families. Third, when mapping designs to workloads, create a short decision rubric: prioritize memory channels for throughput-bound HPC, choose AMX-enabled Xeon variants for INT8 inference, and favor Neoverse for power-efficient cloud scale. Fourth, when analyzing benchmarks, always ask whether a workload is compute-bound, memory-bound, or input and output-bound and tie that back to core count, channels, and PCIe lanes. A common trap is treating benchmark scores in isolation: instead, ask what resource the benchmark stresses. Practicing these small tasks will let you make evidence-based recommendations for server selection.

screens.title: AMD EPYC family overview
screens.narratorSegment: AMD EPYC processors in the Zen 4/Genoa line emphasize high core counts, wide memory bandwidth, and a chiplet-based package. The defining claim is simple: EPYC scales throughput by combining many core-complex dies, or CCDs, with a separate input and output Die to manage memory and peripherals. Practically, a modern EPYC socket can host up to 96 cores in Zen 4c variants and beyond in future generations, with CCDs grouped so eight cores share a 32 MB L3 slice. Memory-wise, EPYC supports twelve DDR5 channels and up to multiple terabytes of main memory, giving it a significant aggregate bandwidth advantage. An example: on a memory-bound HPC workload, many cores need sustained access to DRAM. EPYC's 12-channel design raises the available data rate per socket and reduces the likelihood that cores stall waiting for memory. A common misconception is to assume EPYC's advantage is only core count; in truth, its memory channel count and large shared L3 slices per CCD are equally important to throughput. Another pitfall is thinking cache is always globally shared — EPYC's L3 is shared across a CCD, not across all chiplets; cross-CCD coherence uses a directory. Key takeaway: EPYC is optimized for throughput and memory bandwidth, making it a frequent choice for cloud servers and HPC clusters that favor high parallel throughput. How would you prioritize channels versus cores for your application?

keyIdea.title: EPYC Snapshot
keyIdea.text: Chiplet CCD + IOD design with up to 12 memory channels and large per-CCD L3 to favor throughput and memory-bound workloads.

content.html:
Core Concept

AMD EPYC (Zen 4 / Genoa)

High core counts and a chiplet topology designed to scale memory bandwidth and reduce die reticle limits.

Cores & CCDs
8 cores per CCD; up to 8–12 CCDs per socket in current families.
Memory
12-channel DDR5-4800 for high aggregate bandwidth.
Cache
32 KB L1, 1 MB L2 per core, 32 MB L3 shared per CCD.
I/O
128 PCIe 5.0 lanes; Infinity Fabric interconnect.
Architecture cards
Design explanation
Chiplets reduce yield loss across many cores, and the I/O die centralizes memory controllers and PCIe to simplify CCD design.
Key Takeaway
EPYC targets throughput: more channels and distributed L3 per CCD keep many cores busy on memory-bound workloads.
Common mistake
Equating core count alone to performance without checking memory bandwidth and cache sharing.

screens.title: EPYC chiplet topology: CCDs and the IOD
screens.narratorSegment: The chiplet topology in EPYC packages is a practical response to manufacturing and scaling constraints. The essential claim is that grouping cores into CCDs and separating the input and output functions into a dedicated die allows AMD to scale core counts while keeping yields manageable. Each CCD usually contains eight cores and a 32 MB L3 cache shared among those cores. The input and output Die houses memory controllers and PCIe lanes and connects CCDs using Infinity Fabric in a mesh-like topology. This organization creates two important behaviors: first, intra-CCD cache access is fast because cores within a CCD share a large L3 slice and can use snoop-based coherence. Second, inter-CCD coherence is directory-based and goes through the fabric and input and output die which adds latency relative to intra-CCD traffic. A concrete scenario: a parallel simulation that frequently shares large working sets across many threads may see lower effective bandwidth for cross-CCD accesses because of directory lookups, even though aggregate memory bandwidth is high. A common misconception is thinking all caches are globally uniform; with chiplets, L3 is local to a CCD and that locality impacts miss rates and cross-core latency. The takeaway is to consider thread placement and memory affinity in EPYC systems to keep communicating threads within the same CCD when possible. How might you profile an application to detect cross-CCD traffic?

keyIdea.title: Chiplet Effects
keyIdea.text: Chiplet partitioning creates local L3 domains and directory-coherent inter-chiplet traffic; thread placement and affinity influence performance.

content.html:
Architecture

CCDs and IOD explained

CCDs group cores with a shared L3. The I/O Die centralizes memory controllers and PCIe connectivity and hosts the directory for cross-chiplet coherence.

Local sharing
Snooping and shared L3 provide low-latency sharing within a CCD.
Directory coherence
Directory-based protocols manage cross-CCD coherence through Infinity Fabric and the IOD.
Key Takeaway
Thread placement and memory affinity can reduce cross-CCD latency and improve throughput.
Concrete example
A multi-threaded simulation with shared data benefits when communicating threads are scheduled on cores within the same CCD to avoid directory lookups between chiplets.
Common mistake
Assuming L3 is uniformly shared across all chiplets; it is L3-per-CCD.
Check your understanding
What profiling signals would show frequent cross-CCD memory accesses?

screens.title: EPYC cache and memory hierarchy
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding EPYC's cache and memory hierarchy starts by listing the levels and their roles: each core has 32 KB L1 instruction and 32 KB L1 data caches and about 1 MB L2 per core for fast local hits. The larger 32 MB L3 slice is shared by the eight cores in a CCD and acts as a near-memory region to reduce DRAM traffic. Beyond caches, EPYC provides twelve DDR5-4800 memory channels per socket, producing a high aggregate memory bandwidth that is critical for throughput workloads. One concrete implication: a workload with many simultaneous memory streams benefits from the wider bus because the per-core effective bandwidth remains higher even as core counts increase. An example: an HPC solver with many concurrent threads streaming large arrays will stress DRAM; with 12 channels, EPYC delivers more total bandwidth and reduces contention per core versus an 8-channel design. A common misconception is that adding larger L3 always solves bandwidth problems; L3 reduces DRAM hits but cannot replace the need for raw channel bandwidth for streaming workloads. Key takeaway: evaluate both local cache sizes and total memory channels together. A useful question is whether your workload is cache-friendly or streaming-heavy, because that determines whether per-core caches or aggregate channel bandwidth dominates performance.

keyIdea.title: Memory Hierarchy Principle
keyIdea.text: Per-core L1/L2 caches plus per-CCD L3 reduce DRAM pressure, but total DDR channel count determines aggregate streaming bandwidth.

content.html:
Definition

Cache & Memory Hierarchy

L1 and L2 provide fast private storage. L3 is larger and shared per CCD. DDR channels provide the long-latency, high-capacity tier.

L1 & L2
32 KB L1I/L1D, 1 MB L2 per core for small, low-latency hits.
L3 (per CCD)
32 MB shared among eight cores to reduce DRAM traffic for shared data.
DDR channels
12-channel DDR5-4800 provides high aggregate bandwidth for streaming workloads.
Concrete example
A data-parallel solver with contiguous memory access benefits more from higher channel count than from a modest increase in shared L3.
Key Takeaway
Cache reduces latency; memory channels scale throughput. Measure which resource your workload stresses.
Common misconception
Believing larger L3 alone cures streaming bandwidth limits; it cannot replace channel bandwidth for large, streaming data.

screens.title: Intel Xeon family overview
screens.narratorSegment: Intel's Xeon Sapphire and Emerald Rapids families use a tile-based approach and on-package bridges to achieve modular scaling. The defining elements are tiles — Intel's chiplet term — connected by EMIB and a mesh interconnect on-die. Intel also provides UPI for multi-socket communication. Cache per core differs slightly from EPYC: Intel commonly provides larger L1D (48 KB) and 2 MB L2 per core, and a shared L3 per tile. One notable differentiator is Intel's integration of AMX, Advanced Matrix Extensions, which provide instruction-level acceleration targeted at low-precision matrix operations that speed inference workloads. An example: when running an INT8 image inference pipeline, AMX can significantly improve throughput relative to scalar core execution by accelerating matrix operations inside the C P U. A common misconception is that AMX makes memory irrelevant; it does not. Accelerators still need data fed from caches and DRAM, so bandwidth matters. The design philosophy for Xeon often emphasizes balanced single-thread performance, strong ecosystem compatibility, and specialized accelerator support. Key takeaway: Intel focuses on a mix of strong per-thread performance and on-chip acceleration for AI inference, so for latency-sensitive or accelerator-bound tasks, Xeon variants are compelling choices. What trade-offs would you consider between single-thread performance and raw core throughput?

keyIdea.text: Tile-based design with EMIB and UPI, larger per-core L1/L2, and AMX for matrix acceleration favoring single-thread and AI inference workloads.

content.html:
Core Concept

Intel Xeon (Sapphire / Emerald Rapids)

Tile-based chip architecture, on-package EMIB bridges, and accelerators like AMX for matrix operations.

Cores & tiles
Up to 64 cores per socket; tiles containing up to 15 cores and shared L3 per tile.
Memory
8-channel DDR5-4800, up to 4 TB per socket.
Accelerators
AMX for matrix ops, DSA for data movement.
I/O
~80 PCIe 5.0 lanes; UPI for multi-socket links.
Example scenario
An enterprise inference node using AMX for INT8 workloads reduces CPU cycles per inference and increases throughput while still relying on cache and memory bandwidth for data delivery.
Key Takeaway
Intel targets single-thread performance and AI acceleration, balancing core performance with specialized extensions.
Common misconception
Believing accelerators remove the need for sufficient memory bandwidth; they still require fast data movement.

screens.title: Intel tile interconnects: EMIB, mesh, and UPI
screens.narratorSegment: Intel connects its tiles using multiple technologies: EMIB provides high-bandwidth chip-to-chip bridges on the package while an on-die mesh connects cores and caches regionally. For multi-socket systems, UPI provides coherent links between sockets. The practical effect is that intra-tile snoop-based coherence is fast, while cross-tile or cross-socket traffic may use directory-assisted mechanisms and link-layer protocols that add latency. Tile boundaries are therefore important to understand when reasoning about latency and cache sharing. A concrete example: a database workload sensitive to single-thread latency will benefit from a tile where the working set remains inside the tile's caches. Conversely, a distributed service that uniformly partitions data across threads may be less sensitive to tile boundaries but will still depend on memory channels and the efficiency of EMIB and UPI for interconnect traffic. A common misconception is to treat the package as a single uniform fabric; instead, examine where snooping applies and where directory/coherent links cross tile or socket boundaries. Key takeaway: performance engineering on Xeon often involves placing latency-critical work to avoid cross-tile or cross-socket hops while leveraging AMX for vectorized paths when appropriate. How would you structure thread placement to minimize cross-tile cache misses?

keyIdea.title: Interconnect Reality
keyIdea.text: EMIB and the on-die mesh create fast intra-tile communication, while UPI links provide multi-socket coherence with higher latency than intra-tile sharing.

content.html:
Architecture

EMIB, mesh & UPI

EMIB bridges tiles on the package; an on-die mesh connects cores regionally; UPI connects sockets coherently in multi-socket systems.

EMIB
High-bandwidth short bridge between tiles on the same package.
Mesh
On-die routing for caches and core traffic.
UPI
Coherent multi-socket links for cross-socket memory access.
Scenario
Low-latency services should be scheduled to minimize cross-tile and cross-socket hops; throughput services can exploit many tiles and EMIB bandwidth.
Key Takeaway
Interconnect topology shapes where latency occurs; use placement and affinity to mitigate cross-hops.
Check your understanding
Which profiling metrics indicate cross-socket traffic versus intra-tile sharing?

screens.title: ARM Neoverse family overview
screens.narratorSegment: ARM Neoverse designs emphasize power efficiency and scalable mesh coherence with CMN-700. The key features to remember are ARM's focus on vector-friendly instruction sets like SVE for high-performance floating point and the support for CXL to expand memory off-die coherently. Neoverse families include high-performance and efficiency variants — for example V2 prioritizes performance with wide SVE units, and N2 aims for efficient throughput. These cores can be used in monolithic or chiplet packages and scale to high core counts, supporting up to 128 cores per socket in some implementations. A concrete example: a cloud provider deploying ARM-based nodes may choose Neoverse V2 variants for compute-intensive cloud workloads that benefit from SVE vectorization while relying on CXL to flexibly expand memory capacity for large datasets. A common misconception is that ARM's power efficiency implies lower absolute performance; in fact, with vector SVE and CXL memory expansion, ARM can match or exceed server-class performance for many workloads while consuming less power. Key takeaway: Neoverse is attractive where energy per operation and coherent memory expansion matter, such as large cloud fleets and energy-aware HPC. How would you weigh power efficiency against accelerator availability for your deployment?

keyIdea.text: Coherent mesh (CMN-700), SVE vector support, and CXL memory expansion make ARM Neoverse a power-efficient server option.

content.html:
Core Concept

ARM Neoverse (V2, V3, N2)

Mesh coherence with CMN-700, SVE vector extensions, and CXL for memory expansion drive Neoverse choices.

Cores & vector
SVE-256 or SVE-128 depending on profile, up to high core counts.
Memory & CXL
8-channel DDR5 with CXL for memory pooling and expansion.
Interconnect
CMN-700 coherent mesh on-die for directory-based coherence.
Targets
Cloud servers, HPC, and edge AI where power efficiency matters.
Concrete example
A cloud fleet using Graviton-style instances can leverage SVE-accelerated floating point for cost-efficient compute while using CXL to elastically add memory for large in-memory services.
Key Takeaway
ARM Neoverse balances vector performance and power efficiency, with CXL enabling flexible memory architectures.
Common misconception
Thinking ARM is inherently lower-performing; with SVE and CXL, it can be competitive for many server tasks.

screens.title: CMN-700 and CXL: scalable coherence and memory expansion
screens.narratorSegment: CMN-700 is ARM's coherent mesh that provides directory-based coherence across clusters and memory controllers. The claim here is that a coherent on-die mesh enables a scalable many-core system where directory entries track distributed ownership, reducing global broadcast snoops. Pairing CMN-700 with CXL allows ARM systems to extend memory beyond native DDR channels through a coherent interconnect, enabling memory pooling and disaggregated architectures. Practically, this means a server can attach additional DRAM or accelerator memory via CXL and maintain coherent access patterns. Concrete example: a cloud provider can provision nodes with modest local DRAM and attach larger shared memory pools via CXL when a workload needs large in-memory datasets. This enables better memory utilization across a fleet. A common misconception is that CXL simply adds raw capacity; instead, CXL 3.0 also offers topologies for memory pooling and coherent memory sharing which changes how you architect scaling. The takeaway is that Neoverse combined with CXL supports flexible memory trade-offs — you can scale memory independently of local channel count while relying on CMN-700 for coherence. Ask yourself: which workloads in your environment would benefit most from memory disaggregation?

keyIdea.text: CMN-700 provides directory coherence; CXL enables coherent memory expansion and pooling for flexible server architectures.

content.html:
Process Flow

CMN-700 + CXL

CMN-700 provides coherent on-die paths. CXL lets systems add coherent off-die memory for pooling and expansion.

Directory-based coherence
Tracks ownership to avoid global snoops while scaling cores.
CXL expansion
Adds coherent memory pools that systems can share or expand into.
Concrete scenario
An analytics platform can attach CXL memory to handle peak in-memory aggregation without over-provisioning local DRAM across all servers.
Key Takeaway
CXL plus CMN-700 enables flexible, coherent memory architectures where capacity scales independently from core sockets.
Common misconception
Assuming CXL only increases capacity; it also changes memory topology and sharing semantics.

screens.title: Cache coherence strategies compared
screens.narratorSegment: Across these families we see a common pattern: snooping coherence is efficient for small, tightly-coupled domains, while directory-based coherence scales better across larger, distributed domains like chiplets or tiles. EPYC uses snooping within a CCD and directory-based coherence between CCDs, often mediated by the input and output die and Infinity Fabric. Intel similarly snoops within tiles and uses directory or protocol-assisted coherence across tiles and sockets via UPI. ARM's CMN-700 uses a directory-based mesh to maintain coherence across many clusters. The practical implication is that intra-domain sharing is low-latency and efficient, but when data migrates across domains the cost is higher due to directory lookup and potential remote reads. A concrete example: a multithreaded application that frequently writes shared small structures will be fastest when threads are colocated within the same snoop domain. If the same threads span chiplets or tiles, directory traffic increases and latency rises. A common misconception is to assume coherence cost is uniform; it is not. Performance engineers must measure domain-crossing events and consider thread scheduling, memory placement, and the processor's coherence organization. Key takeaway: optimize for domain-locality when possible, and use profiling to reveal cross-domain coherence bottlenecks. How could you redesign a parallel algorithm to reduce cross-domain coherence traffic?

keyIdea.title: Coherence Trade-off
keyIdea.text: Snooping is fast within small domains; directory coherence scales across chiplets/tiles but adds cross-domain latency that affects shared-data performance.

content.html:
Comparison

Snooping vs Directory

Snooping is efficient inside CCDs or tiles; directory coherence enables scaling across chiplets and sockets at the cost of added latency.

Snooping (intra-domain)
Low latency for small-scale sharing inside CCDs or tiles.
Directory (inter-domain)
Scales across chiplets; incurs directory lookup and remote access costs.
Example
A shared counter updated by many threads benefits from placing threads in the same snoop domain to avoid remote coherence traffic.
Key Takeaway
Profile coherence events and reduce cross-domain sharing to minimize latency and bandwidth pressure.
Common mistake
Assuming coherence costs are identical across all cache accesses; domain boundaries matter.

screens.title: Memory channels, PCIe lanes, and I/O trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: One of the clearest architectural differences across families is the number of memory channels and PCIe lanes per socket. EPYC provides twelve DDR5 channels and about 128 PCIe 5.0 lanes. Intel Xeon typically offers eight DDR5 channels and around 80 PCIe lanes. ARM Neoverse systems often present eight channels and can rely on CXL for expansion, while matching or exceeding PCIe lane counts depending on implementation. These hardware counts translate directly into practical trade-offs: more memory channels increase raw memory bandwidth, helping throughput-bound workloads; more PCIe lanes support larger numbers of accelerators and NVMe devices. A concrete comparison: for a database server that needs many NVMe drives and moderate memory capacity, EPYC's larger lane count is beneficial; for a machine learning inference server that needs integrated accelerators, Intel's AMX plus sufficient PCIe lanes or Neoverse's CXL expansion may be more relevant. A common misconception is to treat channel and lane counts independently; they jointly determine system balance and platform cost. The takeaway is to match the platform's channels and lanes to your application's input and output and memory needs rather than defaulting to the highest core count. Which resource constraint dominates your workload: memory bandwidth or input and output density?

keyIdea.title: Platform Balance
keyIdea.text: Memory channels set bandwidth; PCIe lanes set I/O and accelerator capacity. Choose platforms by the resource your workload needs most.

content.html:
Comparison

Channels & PCIe lanes

EPYC: 12 channels / 128 PCIe. Xeon: 8 channels / ~80 PCIe. Neoverse: 8 channels and CXL options; PCIe varies by implementation.

Memory-bound apps
Benefit from more DDR channels for sustained throughput.
I/O-bound apps
Need more PCIe lanes for NVMe, RDMA, and accelerators.
Scenario
A storage-dense database server may prefer EPYC for its PCIe lane count and memory bandwidth, while an inference server might prioritize accelerator support and AMX on Xeon.
Key Takeaway
Match memory and I/O resources to your workload's dominant bottleneck rather than choosing by core count alone.
Common misconception
Assuming more cores automatically provide more I/O or memory bandwidth; platform specs must be checked.

screens.title: Performance on parallel benchmarks
screens.narratorSegment: Benchmarks reveal how architectural resources translate into workload performance. The chapter summarizes general patterns: all three families can achieve high throughput on SPEC rate tests when many cores are available. For HPCG, which is memory-bound, EPYC and Neoverse typically excel due to higher memory bandwidth and larger shared caches. MLPerf inference results favor Intel Xeon with AMX for INT8 workloads, while EPYC and Neoverse compete strongly for FP32/FP16 tasks. For OLTP/OLAP databases like TPC-C and TPC-H, EPYC's higher core counts and bandwidth often yield strong throughput, while Intel's stronger single-thread latency can benefit latency-sensitive transactional queries. A concrete example: if you run an FP32-heavy scientific simulation that streams large arrays, EPYC's 12 channels and abundant L3 per CCD give it an edge on HPCG. Conversely, a low-latency inference endpoint using INT8 runs faster on Xeon with AMX. A common pitfall is interpreting a single benchmark score as universally representative. Instead, inspect which resource the benchmark stresses: compute, memory bandwidth, or input and output. Key takeaway: pick the processor that aligns the hardware resource stressed by your benchmark with the architecture features the vendor provides. What benchmark best reflects your application's primary bottleneck?

keyIdea.text: Choose benchmarks that stress the same resources your application needs; map results to channels, caches, and accelerators to guide selection.

Process Flow

Benchmarks → Architecture

SPEC rate shows throughput scaling with cores. HPCG highlights memory bandwidth. MLPerf reveals impact of accelerators like AMX and SVE.

HPCG
Memory-bound; favors EPYC and Neoverse with high bandwidth.
MLPerf
INT8 inference often benefits from Intel AMX; FP workloads depend on SVE or FP units.
Concrete application
For a distributed database, measure both throughput and tail latency. EPYC may lead throughput; Xeon may reduce latency for transaction-critical paths.
Key Takeaway
Match the benchmark to your bottleneck and read vendor architecture features to explain differences in scores.
Common mistake
Treating a single benchmark as a universal measure of performance rather than a workload-specific indicator.

screens.title: Mapping workloads to processor families
screens.narratorSegment: Selecting a processor family depends on identifying what resource your workload stresses and then matching that to the platform's strengths. Start with a simple rubric: classify your workload as throughput-bound, latency-sensitive, or accelerator-bound. If throughput and memory bandwidth dominate — for example, scale-out HPC or parallel cloud compute — EPYC's high core counts and 12 memory channels are compelling. If single-thread latency and inference acceleration are critical, Intel Xeon's per-core performance and AMX support can provide lower latency and greater INT8 inference throughput. If energy efficiency and coherent memory expansion matter at scale, ARM Neoverse with SVE and CXL is attractive. Concrete example: a web server handling thousands of concurrent connections that are largely input and output-bound and lightweight may favor EPYC for its socket throughput and PCIe lanes to connect many NICs. A scientific simulation that streams large arrays maps to EPYC or Neoverse depending on vectorization and power budget. An inference farm processing INT8 images may choose Xeon variants with AMX. A typical misconception is thinking the 'best' chip is universally best; instead, use this rubric and map architecture features to your workload. Key takeaway: identify the primary bottleneck, then select the architecture that supplies the resource to relieve it. Which resource will you prioritize for your next deployment?

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we study three families that shape modern servers: AMD EPYC, Intel Xeon, and ARM Neoverse. You will learn the defining architectural choices for each family — chiplets and Infinity Fabric for EPYC, tile and EMIB design plus AMX for Intel, and coherent mesh plus CXL expansion for ARM — and why those choices make a processor suitable for cloud, HPC, or AI workloads. We'll connect concrete hardware facts, like core counts, memory channels, and cache organizations, to practical outcomes: throughput on parallel benchmarks, latency for single-thread work, and efficiency for AI inference. As you explore, notice recurring trade-offs: raw core count versus single-thread performance, memory bandwidth versus input and output density, and the presence or absence of specialized accelerators. A concrete example: EPYC's 12 DDR5 channels support many cores in throughput-bound workloads, while Intel's AMX provides instruction-level acceleration for low-precision inference tasks. Common misconceptions to avoid are thinking more cores always give better performance and assuming AI acceleration replaces the need for memory bandwidth. By the end, you should be able to explain why a cloud provider might pick EPYC for throughput, Intel for mixed latency-plus-AI workloads, or ARM for power-sensitive large-scale deployments. Which design trade-off will matter most for your workload?

By the end of these screens you will have four concrete competencies that map directly to real decisions in system design. First, you will be able to describe the architectures of AMD EPYC, Intel Xeon, and ARM Neoverse using their defining terms: CCD and IOD for EPYC, tiles and EMIB for Intel, and CMN-700 plus CXL for ARM. That means you can explain how cores and on-die caches are packaged and connected. Second, you will compare cache coherence, memory hierarchies, and interconnect topologies across these families so you can justify why one design gives higher bandwidth or lower latency. Third, you will understand which design decisions — for example, EPYC's higher memory channel count or Intel's AMX — make a family better for cloud throughput, AI inference, or single-thread latency. Fourth, you will analyze performance characteristics on parallel benchmarks and translate those numbers into workload recommendations. A concrete example: using channel counts and shared L3 sizes to argue why EPYC often outperforms on memory-bound HPC workloads. A common misconception to avoid is equating core count directly with application speed; instead, consider memory bandwidth, cache sharing, and accelerators. Each card below maps a verified milestone to practice.

This second objectives screen turns the learning targets into practical steps you can perform. First, after you can describe architectures, practice by annotating a processor's datasheet: identify CCDs, tiles, or the CMN-700 and list memory channels. That skill matters because it lets you spot bandwidth bottlenecks early. Second, for coherence and memory, practice comparing directory-based coherence and snooping: determine which domain uses a directory (between chiplets/tiles) and where snooping provides fast intra-die sharing. This clarifies why some workloads see lower cache miss penalties on certain families. Third, when mapping designs to workloads, create a short decision rubric: prioritize memory channels for throughput-bound HPC, choose AMX-enabled Xeon variants for INT8 inference, and favor Neoverse for power-efficient cloud scale. Fourth, when analyzing benchmarks, always ask whether a workload is compute-bound, memory-bound, or input and output-bound and tie that back to core count, channels, and PCIe lanes. A common trap is treating benchmark scores in isolation: instead, ask what resource the benchmark stresses. Practicing these small tasks will let you make evidence-based recommendations for server selection.

AMD EPYC processors in the Zen 4/Genoa line emphasize high core counts, wide memory bandwidth, and a chiplet-based package. The defining claim is simple: EPYC scales throughput by combining many core-complex dies, or CCDs, with a separate input and output Die to manage memory and peripherals. Practically, a modern EPYC socket can host up to 96 cores in Zen 4c variants and beyond in future generations, with CCDs grouped so eight cores share a 32 MB L3 slice. Memory-wise, EPYC supports twelve DDR5 channels and up to multiple terabytes of main memory, giving it a significant aggregate bandwidth advantage. An example: on a memory-bound HPC workload, many cores need sustained access to DRAM. EPYC's 12-channel design raises the available data rate per socket and reduces the likelihood that cores stall waiting for memory. A common misconception is to assume EPYC's advantage is only core count; in truth, its memory channel count and large shared L3 slices per CCD are equally important to throughput. Another pitfall is thinking cache is always globally shared — EPYC's L3 is shared across a CCD, not across all chiplets; cross-CCD coherence uses a directory. Key takeaway: EPYC is optimized for throughput and memory bandwidth, making it a frequent choice for cloud servers and HPC clusters that favor high parallel throughput. How would you prioritize channels versus cores for your application?

The chiplet topology in EPYC packages is a practical response to manufacturing and scaling constraints. The essential claim is that grouping cores into CCDs and separating the input and output functions into a dedicated die allows AMD to scale core counts while keeping yields manageable. Each CCD usually contains eight cores and a 32 MB L3 cache shared among those cores. The input and output Die houses memory controllers and PCIe lanes and connects CCDs using Infinity Fabric in a mesh-like topology. This organization creates two important behaviors: first, intra-CCD cache access is fast because cores within a CCD share a large L3 slice and can use snoop-based coherence. Second, inter-CCD coherence is directory-based and goes through the fabric and input and output die which adds latency relative to intra-CCD traffic. A concrete scenario: a parallel simulation that frequently shares large working sets across many threads may see lower effective bandwidth for cross-CCD accesses because of directory lookups, even though aggregate memory bandwidth is high. A common misconception is thinking all caches are globally uniform; with chiplets, L3 is local to a CCD and that locality impacts miss rates and cross-core latency. The takeaway is to consider thread placement and memory affinity in EPYC systems to keep communicating threads within the same CCD when possible. How might you profile an application to detect cross-CCD traffic?

Understanding EPYC's cache and memory hierarchy starts by listing the levels and their roles: each core has 32 KB L1 instruction and 32 KB L1 data caches and about 1 MB L2 per core for fast local hits. The larger 32 MB L3 slice is shared by the eight cores in a CCD and acts as a near-memory region to reduce DRAM traffic. Beyond caches, EPYC provides twelve DDR5-4800 memory channels per socket, producing a high aggregate memory bandwidth that is critical for throughput workloads. One concrete implication: a workload with many simultaneous memory streams benefits from the wider bus because the per-core effective bandwidth remains higher even as core counts increase. An example: an HPC solver with many concurrent threads streaming large arrays will stress DRAM; with 12 channels, EPYC delivers more total bandwidth and reduces contention per core versus an 8-channel design. A common misconception is that adding larger L3 always solves bandwidth problems; L3 reduces DRAM hits but cannot replace the need for raw channel bandwidth for streaming workloads. Key takeaway: evaluate both local cache sizes and total memory channels together. A useful question is whether your workload is cache-friendly or streaming-heavy, because that determines whether per-core caches or aggregate channel bandwidth dominates performance.

Intel's Xeon Sapphire and Emerald Rapids families use a tile-based approach and on-package bridges to achieve modular scaling. The defining elements are tiles — Intel's chiplet term — connected by EMIB and a mesh interconnect on-die. Intel also provides UPI for multi-socket communication. Cache per core differs slightly from EPYC: Intel commonly provides larger L1D (48 KB) and 2 MB L2 per core, and a shared L3 per tile. One notable differentiator is Intel's integration of AMX, Advanced Matrix Extensions, which provide instruction-level acceleration targeted at low-precision matrix operations that speed inference workloads. An example: when running an INT8 image inference pipeline, AMX can significantly improve throughput relative to scalar core execution by accelerating matrix operations inside the C P U. A common misconception is that AMX makes memory irrelevant; it does not. Accelerators still need data fed from caches and DRAM, so bandwidth matters. The design philosophy for Xeon often emphasizes balanced single-thread performance, strong ecosystem compatibility, and specialized accelerator support. Key takeaway: Intel focuses on a mix of strong per-thread performance and on-chip acceleration for AI inference, so for latency-sensitive or accelerator-bound tasks, Xeon variants are compelling choices. What trade-offs would you consider between single-thread performance and raw core throughput?

Intel connects its tiles using multiple technologies: EMIB provides high-bandwidth chip-to-chip bridges on the package while an on-die mesh connects cores and caches regionally. For multi-socket systems, UPI provides coherent links between sockets. The practical effect is that intra-tile snoop-based coherence is fast, while cross-tile or cross-socket traffic may use directory-assisted mechanisms and link-layer protocols that add latency. Tile boundaries are therefore important to understand when reasoning about latency and cache sharing. A concrete example: a database workload sensitive to single-thread latency will benefit from a tile where the working set remains inside the tile's caches. Conversely, a distributed service that uniformly partitions data across threads may be less sensitive to tile boundaries but will still depend on memory channels and the efficiency of EMIB and UPI for interconnect traffic. A common misconception is to treat the package as a single uniform fabric; instead, examine where snooping applies and where directory/coherent links cross tile or socket boundaries. Key takeaway: performance engineering on Xeon often involves placing latency-critical work to avoid cross-tile or cross-socket hops while leveraging AMX for vectorized paths when appropriate. How would you structure thread placement to minimize cross-tile cache misses?

ARM Neoverse designs emphasize power efficiency and scalable mesh coherence with CMN-700. The key features to remember are ARM's focus on vector-friendly instruction sets like SVE for high-performance floating point and the support for CXL to expand memory off-die coherently. Neoverse families include high-performance and efficiency variants — for example V2 prioritizes performance with wide SVE units, and N2 aims for efficient throughput. These cores can be used in monolithic or chiplet packages and scale to high core counts, supporting up to 128 cores per socket in some implementations. A concrete example: a cloud provider deploying ARM-based nodes may choose Neoverse V2 variants for compute-intensive cloud workloads that benefit from SVE vectorization while relying on CXL to flexibly expand memory capacity for large datasets. A common misconception is that ARM's power efficiency implies lower absolute performance; in fact, with vector SVE and CXL memory expansion, ARM can match or exceed server-class performance for many workloads while consuming less power. Key takeaway: Neoverse is attractive where energy per operation and coherent memory expansion matter, such as large cloud fleets and energy-aware HPC. How would you weigh power efficiency against accelerator availability for your deployment?

CMN-700 is ARM's coherent mesh that provides directory-based coherence across clusters and memory controllers. The claim here is that a coherent on-die mesh enables a scalable many-core system where directory entries track distributed ownership, reducing global broadcast snoops. Pairing CMN-700 with CXL allows ARM systems to extend memory beyond native DDR channels through a coherent interconnect, enabling memory pooling and disaggregated architectures. Practically, this means a server can attach additional DRAM or accelerator memory via CXL and maintain coherent access patterns. Concrete example: a cloud provider can provision nodes with modest local DRAM and attach larger shared memory pools via CXL when a workload needs large in-memory datasets. This enables better memory utilization across a fleet. A common misconception is that CXL simply adds raw capacity; instead, CXL 3.0 also offers topologies for memory pooling and coherent memory sharing which changes how you architect scaling. The takeaway is that Neoverse combined with CXL supports flexible memory trade-offs — you can scale memory independently of local channel count while relying on CMN-700 for coherence. Ask yourself: which workloads in your environment would benefit most from memory disaggregation?

Across these families we see a common pattern: snooping coherence is efficient for small, tightly-coupled domains, while directory-based coherence scales better across larger, distributed domains like chiplets or tiles. EPYC uses snooping within a CCD and directory-based coherence between CCDs, often mediated by the input and output die and Infinity Fabric. Intel similarly snoops within tiles and uses directory or protocol-assisted coherence across tiles and sockets via UPI. ARM's CMN-700 uses a directory-based mesh to maintain coherence across many clusters. The practical implication is that intra-domain sharing is low-latency and efficient, but when data migrates across domains the cost is higher due to directory lookup and potential remote reads. A concrete example: a multithreaded application that frequently writes shared small structures will be fastest when threads are colocated within the same snoop domain. If the same threads span chiplets or tiles, directory traffic increases and latency rises. A common misconception is to assume coherence cost is uniform; it is not. Performance engineers must measure domain-crossing events and consider thread scheduling, memory placement, and the processor's coherence organization. Key takeaway: optimize for domain-locality when possible, and use profiling to reveal cross-domain coherence bottlenecks. How could you redesign a parallel algorithm to reduce cross-domain coherence traffic?

One of the clearest architectural differences across families is the number of memory channels and PCIe lanes per socket. EPYC provides twelve DDR5 channels and about 128 PCIe 5.0 lanes. Intel Xeon typically offers eight DDR5 channels and around 80 PCIe lanes. ARM Neoverse systems often present eight channels and can rely on CXL for expansion, while matching or exceeding PCIe lane counts depending on implementation. These hardware counts translate directly into practical trade-offs: more memory channels increase raw memory bandwidth, helping throughput-bound workloads; more PCIe lanes support larger numbers of accelerators and NVMe devices. A concrete comparison: for a database server that needs many NVMe drives and moderate memory capacity, EPYC's larger lane count is beneficial; for a machine learning inference server that needs integrated accelerators, Intel's AMX plus sufficient PCIe lanes or Neoverse's CXL expansion may be more relevant. A common misconception is to treat channel and lane counts independently; they jointly determine system balance and platform cost. The takeaway is to match the platform's channels and lanes to your application's input and output and memory needs rather than defaulting to the highest core count. Which resource constraint dominates your workload: memory bandwidth or input and output density?

Benchmarks reveal how architectural resources translate into workload performance. The chapter summarizes general patterns: all three families can achieve high throughput on SPEC rate tests when many cores are available. For HPCG, which is memory-bound, EPYC and Neoverse typically excel due to higher memory bandwidth and larger shared caches. MLPerf inference results favor Intel Xeon with AMX for INT8 workloads, while EPYC and Neoverse compete strongly for FP32/FP16 tasks. For OLTP/OLAP databases like TPC-C and TPC-H, EPYC's higher core counts and bandwidth often yield strong throughput, while Intel's stronger single-thread latency can benefit latency-sensitive transactional queries. A concrete example: if you run an FP32-heavy scientific simulation that streams large arrays, EPYC's 12 channels and abundant L3 per CCD give it an edge on HPCG. Conversely, a low-latency inference endpoint using INT8 runs faster on Xeon with AMX. A common pitfall is interpreting a single benchmark score as universally representative. Instead, inspect which resource the benchmark stresses: compute, memory bandwidth, or input and output. Key takeaway: pick the processor that aligns the hardware resource stressed by your benchmark with the architecture features the vendor provides. What benchmark best reflects your application's primary bottleneck?

Selecting a processor family depends on identifying what resource your workload stresses and then matching that to the platform's strengths. Start with a simple rubric: classify your workload as throughput-bound, latency-sensitive, or accelerator-bound. If throughput and memory bandwidth dominate — for example, scale-out HPC or parallel cloud compute — EPYC's high core counts and 12 memory channels are compelling. If single-thread latency and inference acceleration are critical, Intel Xeon's per-core performance and AMX support can provide lower latency and greater INT8 inference throughput. If energy efficiency and coherent memory expansion matter at scale, ARM Neoverse with SVE and CXL is attractive. Concrete example: a web server handling thousands of concurrent connections that are largely input and output-bound and lightweight may favor EPYC for its socket throughput and PCIe lanes to connect many NICs. A scientific simulation that streams large arrays maps to EPYC or Neoverse depending on vectorization and power budget. An inference farm processing INT8 images may choose Xeon variants with AMX. A typical misconception is thinking the 'best' chip is universally best; instead, use this rubric and map architecture features to your workload. Key takeaway: identify the primary bottleneck, then select the architecture that supplies the resource to relieve it. Which resource will you prioritize for your next deployment?

Let's summarize the most important architectural patterns you saw. First, AMD EPYC adopts a CCD + IOD chiplet topology with per-CCD shared L3 and 12 DDR5 channels to favor throughput and memory-bound workloads. Second, Intel Xeon uses tiles, EMIB, and UPI with larger per-core L1/L2 and AMX accelerators to improve single-thread performance and INT8 inference throughput. Third, ARM Neoverse leverages the CMN-700 coherent mesh, SVE vector extensions, and CXL memory expansion to deliver power-efficient scale and flexible memory architectures. A common thread is the mix of snoop-based coherence inside domains and directory-based coherence across domains, which affects latency and placement decisions. As a quick example, keep communicating threads inside the same snoop domain to minimize cross-domain directory lookups. What piece of this summary best aligns with your next experiment?
